utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Good morning to everybody in and around the courtroom. Madam Registrar, will you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning to everyone in and around the courtroom. This is case number IT-04-81-T, The Prosecutor versus Momcilo Perisic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Could we have appearances for today, please, starting with the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning to everybody in and around the courtroom. Dan Saxon, Barney Thomas, and Carmela Javier for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. And for the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone. Daniela Tasic, Chad Mair, Tina Drolec, Novak Lukic, and Gregor Guy-Smith on behalf of Momcilo Perisic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Guy-Smith. Mr. Thomas.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. I called Dr. Michael Williams, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: And just as Dr. Williams is being brought to the courtroom, Your Honours, I can advise that he is a 92 ter witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Thomas.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Good morning, sir.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good morning to you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Will you please make the declaration, sir.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much. You may now be seated.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Thomas.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: Dr. Williams, are you sitting as comfortably as you can be?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL CHARLES WILLIAMS
utterances.text: I am, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: I see that you don't have any blank sheets of paper in front you. You are entitled to make notes if you need to, at any time. Please just let us know if you would like to raise that opportunity.

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL CHARLES WILLIAMS
utterances.text: I would appreciate a piece of note paper, if I may.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Usher.

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL CHARLES WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: Sir, can you begin, please, by giving us your full name and your date of birth?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL CHARLES WILLIAMS
utterances.text: My name is Michael Charles Williams, and my date of birth is 11 June 1949.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: And what is your current occupation?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL CHARLES WILLIAMS
utterances.text: I'm an under-secretary general of the United Nations. I'm currently special coordinator for the UN in Lebanon.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: In March of 2000, did you provide a statement to OTP investigators here at the Tribunal?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL CHARLES WILLIAMS
utterances.text: I did, indeed.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: Your Honours, if we could please have 65 ter 09465 on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: Dr. Williams, do you recognise that as the first page of your statement?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL CHARLES WILLIAMS
utterances.text: I do recognise it, and I would confirm that is the witness statement I gave in March 2000.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: Can you confirm that that's your signature which appears at the bottom of that page?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL CHARLES WILLIAMS
utterances.text: I would confirm it is, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: Have you had the opportunity over the past few days to review the contents of that statement?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL CHARLES WILLIAMS
utterances.text: I have. I have reviewed it thoroughly, and I can confirm that it is -- the statement is true in every respect, as I recall.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: If you were asked to comment on the same matters again today, would your comments be the same?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL CHARLES WILLIAMS
utterances.text: The comments would be the same, indeed.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: Your Honours, could that please be admitted as an exhibit, at this stage marked for identification. There is once further redaction which I have agreed with my learned friend following discussion this morning. I'm hopeful that I can arrange for that to be done during some time during the course of the morning and we can have that redaction incorporated and uploaded into e-court before the conclusion of today at which point the status can be changed from marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The document is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number and marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be Exhibit P2371, marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. And, Madam Registrar, could we please have 65 ter number 09466 on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: Dr. Williams, while that is appearing, can you confirm for us that you testified in the case against Slobodan Milosevic in this Tribunal?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL CHARLES WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Yes, I did. I testified against Mr. Milosevic in June 2003.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: If you look at the screen, do you see there the first page of the transcript of your testimony --

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL CHARLES WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Yes, I do. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: Again, sir, have you had the opportunity to review the contents of that transcript over the past few days?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL CHARLES WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Yes, I have, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: Do you confirm the contents of your testimony and of that transcript?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL CHARLES WILLIAMS
utterances.text: I would confirm both, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: As being true and correct, to the best of your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL CHARLES WILLIAMS
utterances.text: True and correct, to the best of my knowledge.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: If you were asked the same questions today, would your answers be the same?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL CHARLES WILLIAMS
utterances.text: They would be, sir, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: Your Honours, again, at this stage I would move for admission of the transcript as an exhibit, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: It is so admitted -- yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Excuse me. There are some difficulties that exist with the transcript as it is constituted, as I understand what is comprised of in a 92 ter package. I had a brief conversation with Mr. Thomas about this issue. One of the things that happens in this transcript, which is not something that we have experienced necessarily before, and certainly not to the extent that we experience it in this transcript, is there is reference made to tabs which are exhibits, which the witness either confirms -- or say what they say, but then the tab itself, the exhibit itself, is not part of this 92 ter package. And, as I understand, it will not be introduced in evidence. There are references made to exhibits by, once again the use of the word "tab" in which sentences of an exhibit are read out and the witness comments either on the sentences for which I have no difficulty, but also on occasion he comments on other matters that are contained in an exhibit which is not before the Chamber. There -- if you -- if you care, can I give you a couple of examples of this so that you see the difficulty that presents itself. At page 22960 the following question is asked, and the following response is given. Starting at line 17: "Now if I can draw your attention to Prosecution Exhibit 470, tab 35."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You said page 229?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: 22960, line 17. "Q. Now if I can draw your attention to Prosecution Exhibit 470, tab 35, does this document corroborate some of your observations regarding the border closure? "A. I'm sorry, Mr. Groome, tab 35? "Q. Yes, tab 35. "A. Yes it does, yes." We do not have introduced in this case, for example, tab 35.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I can allude to a series of others [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers]... which have the same difficulty. Therefore it be would the Defence's objection that the transcript as it is presently constituted is based on facts that are not in evidence and is therefore not a complete rendition whereby the Chamber can make an intelligent determination of what is being said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Thomas.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: Your Honour, first of all, the example that my learned friend cites is an appropriate matter to bring to the Trial Chamber's attention. I appreciate that that particular reference is not a particularly helpful reference at all, in the absence of any further discussion about the exhibit. Throughout the transcript and the reason why the record is not being burdened with the admission of all of these documents, throughout the transcript there is it reference to the subject matter contained within the particular exhibits and the relevant portions, relevant to the questions which are then put to Dr. Williams. I accept that references such as the ones that my learned friend has referred to, and I note that this comes very -- a long way into the transcript, near the end, is one that is not helpful. If it assists my learned friend and assists the Chamber, if he has other references such as those which carry no further comment other than to simply adopted a document which is not before the Trial Chamber, I agree that those references should either be ignored or deleted from the -- from the transcript. I've discussed the matter with my learned friend this morning. One suggestion he had was that we leave the transcript as marked for identification for the moment. He can canvass various matters in cross-examination. If there are any outstanding issues that he has regarding portions of the transcript that are of no assistance in the absence of the exhibit, then we can address those, either by arranging for the exhibit to be tendered or for a necessary deletion to be made from the transcript. It's the Prosecution position that essentially the transcript speaks for itself when one considers the references to the relevant portions of the documents contained within the transcript, and on occasion, where documents are considered to be of assistance to the Trial Chamber, and there are three of those, we propose to tender those exhibits. But I wonder for the moment, Your Honours, I can suggest that the suggestion made by my learned friend to me before proceedings, began this morning be adopted; that we defer any final resolution of this matter until the conclusion of cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I hear him.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I did make that offer to Mr. Thomas before we started the proceedings today. I think that the matter may have to be deferred till after cross-examination and Mr. Thomas and I have an opportunity to go through the -- to go through the transcript with each other, because I'm not going to be doing some of the work of the Prosecution during my cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you so much. 09466 is now admitted in evidence and marked for identification. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours that will be Exhibit P2372, marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. Thank you, Madam Registrar. Your Honours, the tree exhibits I referred to or I have referred to, again I have discussed this matter with my learned friend, there is no need for those to come up on e-court. I can just signal the 65 ter numbers and seek their admission and the allocation of an exhibit number at this stage, if that is acceptable to the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Why do you want to adopt that procedure? Why do we not have to see them?

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: Simply, Your Honours, because I would not be asking for any comment from Dr. Williams on these exhibits. They are commented by him -- commented on by him already in the transcript that is part of the 92 ter package.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: The first of those is 65 ter number 05726. If that could please be admitted as an exhibit, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You said 0?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. And that's admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be Exhibit P2373.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. The next exhibit is 65 ter number 00863.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: That's admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Exhibit P2374, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours, Madam Registrar. And the final, please, is 65 ter number 00864.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: 00864. It is admitted. May it please be admitted.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Exhibit P2375, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. That, for the moment, takes care of the 92 ter package. And I have a brief summary of the evidence contained in that package. From January 1994 until April 1995, Dr. Williams was director of information for UNPROFOR based in Zagreb. During this time he was the senior spokesman for the UN in the former Yugoslavia, and he coordinated its information programme in the region. In this capacity Dr. Williams was one of the most senior civilian UN officials and officially accompanied the Special Representative of the Secretary-General, Mr. Akashi in his talks with government leaders and various factions throughout the region. Among those with whom Dr. Williams met were representatives of the Bosnian Serb political and military leadership, including Dr. Karadzic and General Mladic, as well as representatives of the FRY leadership, including Slobodan Milosevic. In addition to his other sources of information, Dr. Williams observed firsthand the shelling and sniping of Sarajevo by forces of the VRS. He comments upon the deliberate targeting of civilians and the disproportionate use of force by the VRS. In every meetings that Dr. Williams attended with the Bosnian Serb leadership and/or General Mladic, the Bosnian Serb representatives present were made aware of UN concerns regarding the humanitarian situation. Dr. Williams describes the interrelationship among Slobodan Milosevic, Dr. Karadzic, and General Mladic. He comments upon the dependance of the Republika Srpska, upon financial, materiel, and other support from Serbia and describes the difficulty encountered in monitoring the border between the FRY and the Republika Srpska during a period of sanctions imposed by the FRY in 1994, following the rejection of the contact group plan by the Republika Srpska. Cross border helicopter flights at night, between Serbia and the Republika Srpska were a frequent problem and appeared to increase with the implementation of sanctions. Dr. Williams describes also the evidence prior to July 1995 of tangible objective sides signs, that should the VRS take Srebrenica, a humanitarian crisis on a grand scale would follow. Your Honours, that concludes the summary of Dr. Williams' testimony in the 92 ter package. There is a single matter of clarification relating to his statement which I need put to him, and that should conclude my questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: Your Honours, if we could please --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the presiding Judge's microphone please be turned off. There is too much noise. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: Could we please have Exhibit P2371 on the screen. Page 4 of the English, please, paragraph 4. And page 4 of the B/C/S, paragraph 6.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: Dr. Williams, do you see the paragraph beginning with the words: "UNPROFOR were always trying to negotiate a cease-fire ..."

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL CHARLES WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Yes, I do. Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: You make a comment at the end of that paragraph. "We also tried to negotiate greater humanitarian access, particularly to the eastern enclaves and Sarajevo."

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL CHARLES WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: Could you just explain, please, to the Trial Chamber what you mean by the eastern enclaves?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL CHARLES WILLIAMS
utterances.text: By the eastern enclaves, Your Honours, I refer to three of the safe areas; namely, those of Gorazde, Zepa, and Srebrenica. The court may recall that under Security Council Resolution 836 of, I believe, May 1993, six towns in Bosnia were declared safe areas. Three of these, the three I earlier mentioned, were in the east, and presented great difficulty in terms of the UN supplying their populations with food and necessary humanitarian goods.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: Dr. Williams, thank you. That concludes, for the moment, any questions I have for you. Would you please just remain there for questions that my learned friend will have for you.

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL CHARLES WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Guy-Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Good morning, Dr. Williams.

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL CHARLES WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Guy-Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I'd like to start with, if I could, discussing the relationship between Mr. Milosevic and Mr. Mladic and Mr. Karadzic. As I understand your prior testimony, you have -- you've indicated that Mr. Milosevic had influence over the Bosnian Serb leadership, and by that I mean Mr. Karadzic and General Mladic. And that what would occur is that, on occasion, various members of the Bosnian Serb leadership would -- would assemble in Belgrade. And Mr. Milosevic, as the president of the Republic of Serbia, would use his best endeavours to exert [Realtime transcript read in error "excerpt"] what would be political pressure on the Bosnian Serb leadership. Is that a -- is that an accurate statement?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL CHARLES WILLIAMS
utterances.text: I think that is an accurate statement. From time to time Mr. Milosevic did seek to exercise an influence over the Bosnian Serb leadership. I think a distinction can be made between, of course, the political leadership and the military leadership of the Bosnian Serb republic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Understood. And, as a matter of fact, that's probably not particularly surprising that Milosevic was in that position, attempting to exert influential, because at the time Serbia was, in fact, the political power in the -- in that region; correct?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL CHARLES WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Correct, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Let just make sure we correct this before -- you're referring to "exert influence."

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Just so that the stenographer gets it right because twice now, she's write "excerpt."

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And would it be fair to say that during the period of time, there were a fair number of negotiations, bilateral negotiations with both Karadzic and Mladic?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL CHARLES WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Oh, very much so, sir. Very frequently, almost on a monthly basis I would say, in the period I was there from January 1994 to April of 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And as a result of that, your assessment of Mladic was that he had firm control over his forces and had a disciplined military structure; correct?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL CHARLES WILLIAMS
utterances.text: That was the impression I drew, yes. And -- sorry, I heard interpreter there.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: So did I. I think we're back on track.

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL CHARLES WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Oh, good. Yes, and General Mladic, on a number of occasions, demonstrated that he had control over his forces. On at least one occasion talks, for example, that were held in Geneva in June of 1994, he was in direct touch with forces then encircling Gorazde and instructed them to vacate a certain ridge they were occupying, and that instruction was carried through. There was, as far as I could deduce, a clear line of military command and control.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And clearly based on the example you have just given, Mladic exercised that control in, what we could call, both a firm and decisive manner, did he not?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL CHARLES WILLIAMS
utterances.text: On that occasion, certainly.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. Now, there was -- there was another side to General Mladic, was there not, the hot-headed side? The monomaniacal and temperate side?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL CHARLES WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Perhaps that is a fair comment. Again I recall a critical meeting chaired by president Milosevic in Belgrade on 23rd and 24th of April 1994 at the height of the Gorazde crisis when, after 18 hours of discussions, there was a eventual agreement on a cease-fire in Gorazde. And when a French officer, I believe it was General de Lapresle, the military commander of UNPROFOR, said, Look, thank goodness we have this agreement now, Milosevic all of a sudden reacted in a very intemperate manner and said, And you better make sure that this sticks. We cannot tolerate any action by NATO. And his pose was assertive, if not threatening.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Did you mean -- when you said Milosevic, you meant Mladic, did you not?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL CHARLES WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Yes, I did, Mr. Guy-Smith. Thank you very much. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... Thank you. And he also said, I think, at one point something to the effect of, We'll always send two shells for every shell fired by the Muslims?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL CHARLES WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Yes, he did. Generally if there was any firing out of Bosnian territory towards Bosnian Serb held territory, the reaction was and response was quick, and on the whole, I would say disproportionate.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And you became aware obviously in your dealings with General Mladic that -- that any provocation, no matter how slight, was going to result in disproportionate response by him. That was one of the features of this conflict, correct, unfortunate as it may be, obviously?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL CHARLES WILLIAMS
utterances.text: I think that's right, Mr. Guy-Smith. Some of this stemmed from the armaments of the two forces, whereas the VRS, the Bosnian Serb army, for example was very well equipped with artillery. This was not the case on the Bosnian army side, on the Bosniak side. So from the very armaments, it stemmed that the VRS response was often disproportionate.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And there was another aspect to that, which is that when such a response occurred, it became a feature of the conflict that such a response could be used as a political advantage by -- in this situation it would be the Bosnian Muslim side, the side opposite General Mladic. It was one of the things that occurred as between the parties during this time in the conflict.

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL CHARLES WILLIAMS
utterances.text: I'm not quite sure I follow your assumption that this would be used to a political advantage.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Not would be; could be.

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL CHARLES WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Could be, very good. I accept, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And would it be fair to say that you were -- the majority of the time when you were dealing the Bosnian Serbs, you were turning to Milosevic in situations to try to bring his influence to bear upon the Bosnian Serb party to the conflict?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL CHARLES WILLIAMS
utterances.text: That was true. But not all of the time, Mr. Guy-Smith. Often the first recourse of Mr. Akashi, the Special Representative of the Secretary-General, would be to try and deal directly with the Bosnian Serb leadership.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Understood.

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL CHARLES WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Either through discussions in Pale, their capital, or through direct telephone contact. If he felt that he was making no headway in whatever the issue of the day was, then he would sometimes, first of all, inform president Milosevic of this, and then seek his assistance in trying to get some change in behaviour of the Bosnian Serb leadership.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. And based upon what you have just said, I think it would be fair to say that you recognised that Milosevic was in a position where he could bring influence to the table but not control of the parties.

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL CHARLES WILLIAMS
utterances.text: I think that that's probably right, yes. I mean, president Milosevic had no direct political control over the Bosnian Serb leadership. In fact, of course, president Milosevic's leadership, the old league of Yugoslav Communists stemmed from the Yugoslav communist party. There was a direct line of continuity.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL CHARLES WILLIAMS
utterances.text: The Bosnian Serb political leadership by contrast, did not come from Communist origins. They did not share the same political heritage, and in that respect, were different. If I may add, I think it was different with regard to the representative militaries. They did come from the same background; namely, the old JNA, the old Yugoslav national army. And I think because of that, certain bonds, certain relationships still existed.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Understood. With regard to the matter that you just raised which is Milosevic coming from the old league of the Communist -- Yugoslav Communist party, if I'm not mistaken, so did General Mladic?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL CHARLES WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Correct, Mr. Guy-Smith. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And that was a feature of experience that was not shared with president Karadzic; correct?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL CHARLES WILLIAMS
utterances.text: That's correct. For the most part, the Bosnian Serb leadership, as I recall, the key figures, like Karadzic, the late Mr. Koljevic, and so on, they were not part of the old national Yugoslav leadership.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. I'm -- I don't know if you would agree with me about this or not, but obviously those that share the values and experience of what I'll call the university days oftentimes have a -- a language, a library of understanding from which they can both rely, as well as discuss matters with each other in an easier fashion than somebody who has not been galvanized by those years?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL CHARLES WILLIAMS
utterances.text: I think that is a very right assumption, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: There came a time when the borders were closed, and by that I mean the borders of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, and that was as a result of the Serbian -- the Bosnian Serbian rejection of the contact group plan. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL CHARLES WILLIAMS
utterances.text: That's correct, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And when that occurred Milosevic made some kind of comment, and I think you allude to it in your testimony, that this was not Brazil. And I take it that he could keep the borders -- he could keep the borders contained.

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL CHARLES WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Well, I mean, it certainly wasn't Brazil, of course, because Brazil is a huge continental country, as we all know. Nevertheless, the borders between the Bosnian Serb republic and between Serbia proper did present problems for control, and even for observation, the nature of the terrain and the length of the border presented many difficulties.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And with regard to the closing of the border by Milosevic, this was part of a process which was to assist in the imposition of sanctions. And -- correct?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL CHARLES WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Yes, sir, you're correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: The sanctions that were being viewed at that time, certainly from your position, I would think, demonstrated that the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia was seriously against the Bosnian Serb leadership's position at that time; correct?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL CHARLES WILLIAMS
utterances.text: I think by the time that the sanctions are imposed and Mr. Milosevic, president Milosevic, had accepted the contact group plan, there were clear political differences between, as it were, Belgrade and Pale. Having said that, how effective the closure of the borders, well, I think is open to a question mark.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Understood.

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL CHARLES WILLIAMS
utterances.text: I also have to say that my opinion, and not my opinion alone, was that the international community was given grossly inadequate facilities for monitoring that border when it was closed.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. Be that as it may, the imposition of these sanctions and the border closure was a device whereby he was trying to influence again the Bosnian Serb leadership to take -- if we might call it a more constructive or a positive role in the peace process, the one that he had agreed to and adopted. By "he," I'm referring to Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL CHARLES WILLIAMS
utterances.text: That's true, and that's certainly what president Milosevic said to a number of interlocutors at the time; Mr. Stoltenberg from Norway and lord David Owen, as well as Mr. Akashi. He would frequently make rather dismissive remarks about the Bosnian Serb political leadership and find it unfathomable that they did not accept the peace plan that was on offer.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And this was just one of a series of -- series of attempts or engagements on his part to try to restrain them, to influence them, and to bring them into line with his position, the one that you have mentioned, and that being the position of being engaged in the peace process. Correct?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL CHARLES WILLIAMS
utterances.text: That's certainly the impression he gave, and I think there is evidence to indicate that he did try and exert that influence from time to time. However there's always a differences between what is said perhaps in diplomacy and the realities on the ground, how effective he was in instrumentalising the sanctions against the Bosnian Serb republic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: He made the statement, if I'm not mistaken, at one point that, We are for peace. We have made the close of peace, I believe, is a statement that Milosevic had made.

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL CHARLES WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Yes, sir, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. Now, with regard to the -- the events I believe you -- in your testimony you discuss Gorazde; correct?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL CHARLES WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Correct, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Now, with regard to Gorazde, it's your understanding, is it not, that there were no members of the FRY leadership in Gorazde at that time, in April -- I think it would be April of 1994.

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL CHARLES WILLIAMS
utterances.text: No, there were not. At that time, Gorazde, as I indicated earlier, was one of the six towns or cities declared safe areas by the Security Council of the UN. And although it was encircled by Bosnian Serb forces, the town itself was part of the Bosnian republic and had Bosnian republic forces inside it.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. He received, I take it, to your knowledge, information from Karadzic and Mladic concerning what was occurring?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL CHARLES WILLIAMS
utterances.text: He must have done. And one also needs to bear in mind that Gorazde, itself, is very close to the Serbian border. It is no distance at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And with regard to any of the statements that he made in regard to Gorazde, they may or may not be his own assessment in the sense of what he has seen or heard but, rather, based on information that was given to him by, for example, Mladic or Karadzic; correct?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL CHARLES WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And with regard to the issues that you were presented with and the issues that all the parties were presented with, this is one of the common features of these kinds of negotiations, which is oftentimes you're negotiating based upon information that you have received second, third hand. And it's not necessarily either reliable or unreliable, but it's information upon which you have to make a determination that you're going use or not use, based upon the -- shall I put it, this term, the necessity of the moment?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL CHARLES WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Yes. I should clarify that the UN itself did have some officials and observers in the town of Gorazde. For example, there were quite a number of what are called UNMOs, UN Military Observer. The UN High Commission for Refugees, also had several staff members there. And I also had one member of my own office based there. So there was a variety of reporting from the town from UN sources.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. It would be fair to say that at point in time, vis-a-vis your relationship with the Bosnian Serb leadership, and by that I mean the international community, those relationships were, to put it mildly, somewhat strained, were they not?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL CHARLES WILLIAMS
utterances.text: They were strained always when there was military action undertaken by the Bosnian Serb forces, which in the period in which I was present in the former Yugoslavia, I have to say was quite frequent, whether it was Sarajevo or Gorazde or Bihac or some of the eastern enclaves.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And once again, this is another situation in which Milosevic was involved in -- in a series of -- of what I'd call manoeuvres and in an attempt to influence the Bosnian Serb leadership to change their position.

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL CHARLES WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Yes. I mean, I think, you know, some of us felt that although he was trying perhaps to influence that leadership, that he could have done more to be effective in restraining it. One only had to look at the map to realize that the Bosnian Serb republic, its institutions and its military, were very dependant upon Serbia. And there was a feeling that many of us had that Mr. Milosevic, while he did seek to exert his influence from time to time, certainly over Gorazde in the end and over the contact group peace plan, might have done so more strenuously at an earlier date.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: So was his -- his failure to do so at an earlier date something that was discussed with him?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL CHARLES WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Yes, it was. And Mr. Akashi would appeal directly to him, Look, I call upon you to exercise your leadership to -- to restrain the Bosnian Serbs from their repeated attacks on UN Safe Areas.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: When you use the -- when you use the phrase there, "exercise your leadership," I take it that what you're talking about once again is an issue of influence as opposed to an issue of control?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL CHARLES WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Formally speaking, yes, you're absolutely correct. I mean, he did not have political control over the Bosnian Serb leadership. One has to say that there's -- there's a continuum between control and -- and influence. And it's not the case that these were two normal neighbouring countries where one might seek to exercise brotherly influence or give counsel to another. And the Bosnian Serb republic effectively had no functioning economy. Its military, for logistical purposes, was highly dependant upon Serbia. Buts this extended to other areas as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: You just said something here which I find kind of interesting which is, "And it is not the case that these were two normal neighbouring countries where one might seek to exercise brotherly influence or give counsel to one another." As a matter of fact, what we had at the time was quite a unique situation, which is you had the breakup and essentially what I think you would call a civil war between what had once been a -- a large country held together with many different individuals in it and many different factions in it. Not dissimilar perhaps to what occurred in the United States during the civil war.

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL CHARLES WILLIAMS
utterances.text: I mean, there are some similarities. In the US, of course, there was a clear division between north and south, between the union and the confederates. It was different in the former Yugoslavia, because one national state broke up into many republics. And then within some of those republics, particularly within Bosnia, there was for a long time three contending forces; namely, the Bosnian Serb republic, the Bosnian republic based in Sarajevo, but also the Bosnian Croat forces around Mostar. Now after March 1994, there was a Federation between the Bosnian Croat forces and the Bosnian republic in Sarajevo. So it's a complicated picture.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Well, that's precisely what I was driving at. It is a complicated picture. And to the extent that there were old relationships or former alliances, it was those upon which you were relying on, in a certain sense, for purposes of influence which you understood what those limitations would be and could be by virtue of the unique situation in which you found yourself in. True?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL CHARLES WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. I would like to show you a document to see whether or not you have any familiarity with it.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: It's a document, 1D01-0212. It is from -- if we could scroll to the bottom of the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: It is from Major-General Morillon. Do you know who that individual was?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL CHARLES WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Yes, I do, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And who was that individual?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL CHARLES WILLIAMS
utterances.text: He was the -- at the time of this letter he was a commander of the UN forces in Bosnia-Herzegovina, based in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And the letter is addressed to --

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL CHARLES WILLIAMS
utterances.text: President Izetbegovic of the Bosnian republic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: What was the army serving under President Izetbegovic that?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL CHARLES WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Would be the -- the Bosnian Muslim army. I think it's initials were the ABiH.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. And with regard the information that's contained therein, is this a subject that you were familiar with, that an 82-millimetre mortar set up on the western side of Kosevo hospital within the hospital grounds which had then been used to fire nine rounds using the hospital as a screen?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL CHARLES WILLIAMS
utterances.text: I'm familiar with this incident from reports and I've also seen this letter in the UN archives. I should point out that to the Court, however, that this incident was in January 1993 when I was not in Yugoslavia. In fact, at that time, I was with the United Nations in Cambodia.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I understand that. You are familiar with the incident?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL CHARLES WILLIAMS
utterances.text: I am, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. Is the incident here the type of complaint that was made by the Bosnian Serb leadership -- I'm sorry. Yes, by the Bosnian Serb leadership about the activities of the ABiH? And by that, I mean using such things as a hospital as a shield for purposes of waging their part of the war. Whether -- whether or not you -- you put any stock in what was being said or not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I'm just asking the Registrar to scroll this document up. Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, as I mentioned, I was not in Bosnia or the former Yugoslavia at the time. This was a particularly egregious violation of the Geneva Convention. I am not aware of any similar incidents during the time of my service in Bosnia. But such actions can only be thoroughly condemned.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I would like to have this admitted as defendant's next in order, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: This document is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Exhibit D99, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: When you say that you are not familiar with any similar incidents, are you confining that statement to the use of a hospital as a shield?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL CHARLES WILLIAMS
utterances.text: I -- I am, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. Just wanted to make sure that -- I wanted to make sure that -- that we were clear about the extent to which you were -- you were making the point. Did you, in your capacity, receive information about the ABiH having a mobile mortar truck or tank within Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL CHARLES WILLIAMS
utterances.text: I'm not quite sure what you mean by that. But I would say that, you know, mortars by definition are fairly portable weaponry. You can almost fold it up and put it in the back of a car and take it somewhere to fire and then fire off several rounds and then move on somewhere else. It's not like a heavy artillery gun. But that the Bosnian forces had that capability, I would not deny. I mean, that's very true.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL CHARLES WILLIAMS
utterances.text: And that they did use mortar attacks from Sarajevo from time to time.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Did you ever receive any information concerning the -- the troop strength of the ABiH during the time that you were in region?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL CHARLES WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Yes, we did. I mean, it varied, of course, and many of their forces were encircled in the various enclaves.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Yesterday we heard from a witness that the troop strength was in the neighbourhood, I think, of some hundred thousands, or hundreds of thousands; I don't remember exactly the precise figure. I had given him a figure of 230.000, which he rejected. He said it was a bit too high. In your estimation, could you tell us what figures you had. And I understand this -- it's a guesstimate at best, but ...

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL CHARLES WILLIAMS
utterances.text: It would be that, sir. But I would say that even 100.000, I would regard as a sort of upper most.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Thomas.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honours, we went from talking specifically about Sarajevo to troop strength. And I just want to find out from my learned fiend --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Sorry can you just hold on. Yes, Mr. Thomas.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: Just trying to find form learned friend whether the question related to troop strength in Sarajevo, or whether it represented the troop strength in total of the ABiH on the territory.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Before Mr. Thomas rose I saw the difficulty with the question as posed and the answer as given, and I had a follow-up question in mind.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yeah, would you like to clarify that.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: With regard to the troop strength in Sarajevo, could you give us a number? Is that -- is that the 100.000 that is in discussion, or would you believe it to be something different?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL CHARLES WILLIAMS
utterances.text: I would hesitate to comment on this, but and you used it yourself -- Mr. Guy-Smith used the expression of a sort of a guesstimate. I would argue that 100.000 was perhaps the guesstimate for ABiH forces throughout Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I hope that clarifies the issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Did you ever receive any information that the BiH army had barracks near the ice stadium in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL CHARLES WILLIAMS
utterances.text: I do recall some ABiH forces being located near there, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. Is that what --

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL CHARLES WILLIAMS
utterances.text: I do recall ABiH forces being located near there. By the ice stadium -- you mean the ice stadium?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL CHARLES WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Yeah, sorry, it's come up incorrectly on the transcription. These refer to the old winter Olympics facilities in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Precisely. Did you receive information that the ABiH fired mortars close to UN positions at the PTT building?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL CHARLES WILLIAMS
utterances.text: There was that allegation on at least one occasion, I recall. The PTT building would be in the post and telegraph building in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: The HG UNPROFOR? I'm asking the same question about that.

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL CHARLES WILLIAMS
utterances.text: I can't recall a specific example, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: What do you mean by HG?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Do you mean the headquarters?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, HQ.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I misspoke myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: The Tito barracks. Did you hear of?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL CHARLES WILLIAMS
utterances.text: I did not, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. You've mentioned the matter of helicopter flights, and I'd like to spend some time with you there. In that regard, did you receive specific reports of helicopters being flown cross border?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL CHARLES WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Yes, we did, sir. We had reports from UN military observers located in a number of the enclaves in Eastern Bosnia, including Tuzla, of helicopter movements. Sometimes in substantial numbers. Often at night.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And when you received such information, I take it that you made appropriate protestations to the parties concerned?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL CHARLES WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Definitely. The Court will wish to recall that there was no-fly zone in Bosnia-Herzegovina that was imposed upon a request by the Security Council to NATO. So helicopter movements, unless authorised, on occasion they might be authorised, for example, for purpose of medical evacuation, would have been violations of Security Council actions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: This no-flow zone was it Bosnia-Herzegovina-wide?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And with regard to such protestations, did you receive responses, and from that I mean responses from the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, concerning whether or not they had been involved there flying helicopters into the region?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL CHARLES WILLIAMS
utterances.text: There were responses. And there were a number of occasions I have to say when we found the responses of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia authorities to be inaccurate. And, indeed, on at least one occasion, UN military observers who had been deployed on the -- on the FRY side, on the Serbian side of the border, had their access to radars at a Yugoslav air base blocked by security officials there.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Yes, we have heard consider testimony about that particular incident earlier on, and, as a matter of fact, I think we learned, among other things, there was a fair amount of disagreement within the room as to who had what power to do what, which was ultimately ironed out. Is that your recollection as well?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL CHARLES WILLIAMS
utterances.text: I do recall that. I mean, I think it is worth stating before the Court that flying helicopters at night is not an easy matter for any air force, even a very experienced and well equipped air force. It required obviously a lot of coordination with ground communications and with radar. And I'm -- particularly on one occasion I recall that our observers reported the movement of 15 helicopters at night flying easterly towards, I think, Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And with regard no that that particular assertion, was that confirmed by the FRY authorities, or was that rejected by the FRY authorities?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL CHARLES WILLIAMS
utterances.text: To be honest, Mr. Guy-Smith, I cannot recall their precise response on that occasion.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Do you recall as you sit here today any of the discussions and ultimate conclusions that were made with regard to the accuracy of the information concerning helicopter flights? And by that I mean that there were difficulties with some of the machines that were being used.

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL CHARLES WILLIAMS
utterances.text: You mean some of the helicopters themselves, or some of the machines monitoring the helicopter flight?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: The machines monitoring the helicopter flight.

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL CHARLES WILLIAMS
utterances.text: You know, my experience in this fields of conflict is there are often problems with the technical equipment. Having said that, the forces that were doing this monitoring from the ground were forces as part of the UN mission, but their national forces were NATO forces, there were Dutch forces, in particular, I remember Norwegian forces. So these were forces of considerable integrity and considerable technical acumen.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I appreciate that. But it would be fair to say that what was also available was objective information in the sense radar or other tracking devices that would allow for an impartial determination of flight patterns, flight distance, and other associated flight issues, such as direction?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL CHARLES WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. And that's what I'm talking about, is that there were difficulties that were found and ultimately acknowledged by the parties with regards to those particular machines.

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL CHARLES WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Well, you know, there may have been difficulties on a particular night, whether it's, you know, July 7th or February 14th or whatever. And the -- but there was a pattern of aerial activity, and particularly of helicopter activity, which indicated serious violations of the no-flow zone and a possible if not probably concurrence in this activity by FRY authorities.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: You have used the term "pattern of aerial activity," which is a relatively strong term, I would suggest. Could you tell us how many helicopter flights fit into the pattern that you are alluding to here?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL CHARLES WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL CHARLES WILLIAMS
utterances.text: I think my recollection is that in 1995, the frequency of helicopter flights seemed to increase given my recollection of the reports that we had. And particularly in the eastern part of Bosnia. Now, the Bosnian army, the ABiH forces, had a few helicopters, not many, certainly not as many as the Bosnian Serb army had. And a lot of these helicopter flights, as I indicated earlier, were at night, which is no mean feat for any air force or army, and this needed quite some considerable coordination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You indicated a little earlier that on one night 15 helicopters had been sighted.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You're talking of a person -- were they only -- were 15 sighted on one occasion only? Or you say more on -- what kind of number could be seen on more than one occasion?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: To the best of my knowledge, Your Honour, in the period I was in the former Yugoslavia, this was the maximum number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: What would have been the minimum?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The minimum would have been one, two, three, flights. And perhaps that more the norm, sir, than 15.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: What about the regularity?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think in the course of 1995, there were regular flights. It would also be the case, Your Honour, that on some occasions it would have been probable that not all of these flights would have indeed have been picked up by UN radar systems.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: When you say "regular," how regular?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I would not say daily, Your Honour, but I would certainly say that this would be happening several times a week.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: What do you mean by several? Can you give an estimate?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I would have said two, three, four, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Does that answer your question?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Hmm.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: But as you sit here today, you can give us no hard evidence with regard to those helicopter flights that you have alluded to, no documentation, can you?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL CHARLES WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Well, the -- my recollection, Mr. Guy-Smith, is that there was documentation at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I appreciate what you're saying. I'm asking, but as you sit here today?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL CHARLES WILLIAMS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Would this would be an appropriate time?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: It would be indeed. We'll take a break and come back at a quarter to 11.00. Court adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Before you continue, Mr. Guy-Smith, I think the Registrar has something to correct. Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. Earlier today at page 26, line 20, I assigned document number 1D01-0212 to have -- to be Exhibit D99, where the correct number for that document should be Exhibit D100.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much, madam. Yes, Mr. Guy-Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you so much. If we could have 1D00-4766 on the screen, please. And if we could scroll down.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: With regard to the issue of helicopter border crossings between the FRY and Bosnia-Herzegovina, I'd like you to take a look at this particular document, if you could, please. And if you could indicate when you have finished reading the first page, we can move to the second page.

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL CHARLES WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Is it possible to scroll down to the bottom.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Absolutely. Surely.

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL CHARLES WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Oh, okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And if we can move to the second page. And then scroll up.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Before we go any further, are you familiar with this document?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL CHARLES WILLIAMS
utterances.text: I am not, Mr. Guy-Smith. No.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: If we could go to page 5 of the same -- thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: This is a letter, obviously, we can see the date is the 11th of April, 1995, and if we go to the third paragraph, I think it discusses some of the things we discussed previously with regard to FRY's rejection of flights back and forth. It says: "On the basis of extensive investigation, however, the competent Yugoslav authorities can confirm that throughout March 1995 there were only six helicopter flights from the Republika Srpska to the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia and vice versa. The purposes of all those flights was the transport of the critically wounded. Four of those flights were effected with the authorisation of UNPROFOR and two without. Those two were emergency medevac flights that had to be effected since the transportees were in a life-threatening condition, and it was not possible to wait for approval. Other than those, there were no flights from the Republika Srpska to the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia and vice versa." It goes ton say: "It is absolutely excluded that the flights" -- If we scroll down, please. "-- referred to in the report of the co-chairman except the six medevac flights mentioned earlier, were those carried out by the helicopters of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia or the Republika Srpska. The difference in the number of flights observed 26 by the United Nations air field monitors the at Surcin airport and the number which actually took place, 6, can be explained by the UNPROFOR reports regarding parent violations of the ban on flights in the air space of Bosnia and Herzegovina where, on several occasions, it is explicitly stated that the alleged nights above the territory of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia faded away from the screen, and it could not be determined where the helicopters landed." If we could turn to the next page please. "A possible explanation is that what is involved are flights of helicopters of the Bosnian Muslim side which flew from Central Bosnia to the Muslim enclaves in eastern Bosnia close to the border with the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. Such a conclusion is justifiable from the" --

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL CHARLES WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Could you please read slowly.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Yes. "Such a conclusion is justifiable from the technical point of view since it is illogical that the radar of the regional flight control at Surcin airport (Belgrade) is more reliable in directing flights tracks of helicopters at a greater distance (in the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina) than at a shorter one over the territory of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia itself." It goes on to say: "It is also possible that special electronic devices were engaged to deliberately simulate flight patterns and put the blame on the Bosnian Serb or the Yugoslav side. "I should be greatly if you would have the present letter circulated as a document of the Security Council. And it's signed by Dragomir Djokic. Are you familiar with this particular allegation, in terms of their being six helicopter flights, as opposed to 26. Of those six helicopter flights, four were approved by UNPROFOR, two not, because of life-threatening situations?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL CHARLES WILLIAMS
utterances.text: I do remember this document. This, of course, is the explanation put forward by the FRY authorities. Whether it is a plausible explanation is a debatable matter. I would say it was highly problematic. For example, the reference to Bosnian Muslim helicopters possibly going into the eastern enclaves. To the very best of my recollection, throughout my service with UNPROFOR, I was not aware of a single reported flight, not one, into any of the three eastern enclaves, Gorazde, Zepa, and Srebrenica. And I remind the Court that, of course, there were UN forces on the ground in each of those enclaves, which are very, very small areas. And it would be impossible for a helicopter to land without it being noticed in those enclaves by UN forces. So I note the letter, I remember reading it at the time. It's not one of the most convincing letters I have seen sent to the Security Council.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I appreciate your view of the letter. But my question is, rather -- was actually limited to whether or not you were aware of it. You've indicated that you are. Now --

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL CHARLES WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: -- do you know whether there was a subsequent investigation with regard to these particular flights?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And if you do, what the results were. So it's a -- I admit it's a compound question, but ...

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL CHARLES WILLIAMS
utterances.text: I think the answer, sir, is that I'm not aware. I note also that this letter was dated the 11th April. And I left the UN service in Yugoslavia on the 17th of April -- 15th April, sorry, my recollection in 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Could that be admitted as defendant's next in order, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: What do you want to admitted, this one or -- what about the first one which the witness didn't know anything about?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Well, I think that if he didn't know anything about it, under the Rules, it doesn't come in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: So you're tendering this one only.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Yes. I'm tendering pages 5 and 6.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Those pages are admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, pages 5 and 6 of 1D00-4766 will be Exhibit D101.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Were you in -- in contact at all with Mr. Kirudja concerning the issue of helicopters?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL CHARLES WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Yes, sir. Mr. Kirudja was the representative of UNPROFOR in the FRY capital, the Serbian capital, Belgrade. He was a senior official there.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And did you have -- did you have occasion to discuss with him at any point in time what the -- what the ultimate conclusions were made with regard to the whole issue of helicopters?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL CHARLES WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Not -- not the ultimate conclusions, as I recall. I do remember a meeting with him in Zagreb when he was on a visit there to our headquarters, where we discussed the matter. In fact, it was discussed within a sort of senior staff meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. And with regard to you discussing the matter with Mr. Kirudja, did you come to an understanding that the issue of, what I will call, helicopter flight violations was not as great as it seemed but there was some concern?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL CHARLES WILLIAMS
utterances.text: There was a very serious concern. Mr. Kirudja, like myself, was a civilian official of the United Nations, and, of course, the observation of these helicopters, the documentation and so on, was undertaken by our military colleagues, and the evidence was produced by them.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I'm moving to another topic. You, in your testimony, discuss the issue of keeping the air bridge open. Could you, first of all, explain to the Chamber what an air bridge is?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL CHARLES WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Yes, sir. By reference to the air bridge, I refer in particular to the very regular flights between Zagreb and Sarajevo, which were the main connection to the outside world from Sarajevo. And these planes brought UN personnel, civilian and military into Sarajevo. But perhaps more importantly, they also brought supplies, particularly medical supplies, to the besieged city. From time to time there was also a road open to Sarajevo, but the air bridge was pretty critical to the city.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Apart from the air bridge that you've just mentioned, were you cognizant of there being an air bridge between February of 1993 and May of 1995 maintained from the Bosnian-Herzegovinian territory for the needs of Srebrenica, Zepa, and Gorazde?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL CHARLES WILLIAMS
utterances.text: I'm afraid I don't quite follow your question, Mr. Guy-Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Was there -- was there an air bridge to those three areas that I have just mentioned?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL CHARLES WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Okay, sorry. I follow you now.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I apologise if I was confusing.

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL CHARLES WILLIAMS
utterances.text: No, my misunderstanding, too, I think. There were no air fields in these three eastern enclaves; Srebrenica, Zepa, Gorazde, so it was impossible to send in airplanes. Three's eastern enclaves were, therefore, supplied by road. The convoys to these towns would come from either the FRY, UNHCR, for example, convoys went to these three enclaves. But also, on occasion, there were convoys by road from Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Were you aware of the fact that there was an assertion that -- made by ABiH army personnel of the fact that there was an air bridge in which there had been some number of flights, certainly not many, from these areas that had to be maintained?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL CHARLES WILLIAMS
utterances.text: I'm not aware of that assertion. I find it difficult to believe. I mean, three's are very small areas, particularly Zepa. I mean, it's a village. Srebrenica and Gorazde are more substantial. But in both of those places, to the best of my knowledge, there is no air field, no landing strip, let alone what might be called an airport. And in both Srebrenica, Gorazde, there were UN forces. I find it very, very difficult to believe that they would not have noticed air movements directly into very small areas.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: If I could have a moment, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Could we have 1D01-1881 up on the screen. We're struggling to see whether or not -- this document was sent for translation. We're struggling to see whether or not the final translation has in fact been achieved or not, and, if it has, we will try to link it up. I don't know if you speak Bosnian, Croatian, or Serbian, so I'm trying to get --

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL CHARLES WILLIAMS
utterances.text: I do not sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: All right. Well, hopefully we'll be in a position where I can have the final document for you in English. But if not, I'm going to proceed for the moment reading you a rough translation, and if the -- the usher would be kind enough at least to give a copy of this to my colleague so that he can follow along. This is a rough, and by that I mean, very rough translation. I'm not asserting that it is, and we will ask for the actual translation to be linked to the document at the time that we finally receive it. This is a document that I understand comes from the ABiH RV and PVO command, highly confidential, number 08/896-1, Zenica, date 17.02.1995. And it's entitled "Final Analysis of the Work of the Air Bridge for Srebrenica and Zepa, to GS, ABiH, General Enver Hadzihasanovic." Now before we go any further just for purposes of clarity, would you know what the letters GS stand for?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL CHARLES WILLIAMS
utterances.text: I do not. I mean, often it refers to General Staff in military documents. I don't know if that is the case here.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Let us proceed on that assumption. It goes on to say: "Based on your oral order, we hereby deliver you the analysis" --

utterances.speaker: THE COURT REPORTER
utterances.text: Slower please.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Yes, to all that I'm speaking too fast for.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: -- "of the work/functioning of the air bridge for Srebrenica, Zepa, and Gorazde, Deputy Commander Colonel, Hrustic Erdin."

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Could we scroll down to the second page, please. Starting at number 1, introduction. And I understand this may not be an official translation. "In the time-period from 27/2/93 until 7/5/1995, an air bridge is maintained from the RBiH territory for the needs of the Srebrenica, Zepa, and Gorazde enclave. The primary goal of the maintaining of the air bridge was the provision and delivery of a means for conducting combat operations. The evacuation of the wounded, the functioning of the organs of powers in the enclaves, for schooling of the officer Cadre on the liberated territories of RBiH, and for maintaining the communication lines. "The establishment and maintenance of the air bridge has a significance importance in providing the possibility for the defence of the population and the territory in the condition of being fully surrounded and blocked and next to the presence of UNPROFOR, who did not fulfil their obligations under their mandated to protect the civilian population in the territories of the enclaves. The morale of the fighters and the civilian population is greatly boosted, not only because of the provision of UBS and MTS," both of those are acronyms that I'm not in a position at this point to translate, "but also because of the feeling of not being completely abandoned or forgotten, but, rather, that the organs of power RBiH are determined to take any measure to liberate this part of the territory of RBiH. "A great courage was shown by the members of RV and PVO in the establishing and maintaining of this air bridge, in spite of the fact that the aggressor managed to take over the protected zones. What the members of RV and PVO did made it possible for conducting of long lasting combat operations and fight as well as ease the consequences of withdrawal of civilians and the fighters towards the liberated territories of BiH."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Do you intend reading all this document, sir?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: No, I do not.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Section number 2 discusses the main tasks of the air bridge, which includes transporting of weapons and equipment, fighters, material for the functioning of both the military and civilian authorities, maintenance of communication lines, transport of the wounded, and transport of the food. If we could scroll down, please, to, I believe, it's page 10. And page 10 is an annex of the flights giving the date for Srebrenica. Now, my question to you, sir, is obviously this is not a document you have ever seen?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL CHARLES WILLIAMS
utterances.text: No, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I'm clear about that. With regard to the information that is contained within the document, I take it that this is information that you have never been privy to, that there was any kind of, shall we say, air bridge or air support that was being used by the ABiH army?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL CHARLES WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Correct, sir. I mean, I can't comment on the authenticity of this letter at all. I would make two points, however. And as I recall it, on page 1, the date of this letter was reportedly 17th of February, 1995. Then in paragraph 1, for which you only give a rough translation, you -- you note, and it says clearly in the documents, analysis between 27th of February 1995 and 7th of May, 1995, i.e., after the date of the letter itself. So I don't quite understand that anomaly. There seemed to me other possible anomalies. But then finally the data you referred to at the end, the alleged helicopter flights into Srebrenica. I notice that all ten of those flights occur in a period of one month, they are all between the 27th of February, 1993, and 30th of March, 1993. Now I was not in the Former Yugoslavia during that period. I could not comment at all on that. They may or may not have taken place. What I would say, again, is that during the period that I was there, from January 1994 to April of 1995, I am not aware of a single flight into any of these -- the three eastern enclaves, Srebrenica, Zepa, Gorazde. That was noted by the UN forces on the ground. Indeed, I find it very, very difficult to accept that there would have been a flight. Again, I repeat for the Court, I don't -- an aeroplane could certainly not have gone into those places. A helicopter, possibly. The Court also perhaps should be aware that, you know, during this period, Gorazde itself, particularly in March/April 1994, was critically under attack from the Bosnian Serb forces. I mean, it would have been unfathomable then that a Bosnian army helicopter would have managed somehow to got in through the Bosnian Serb attack on the town. So I -- I have to say that I'm pretty skeptical of this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. I understand you're skeptical of the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: With regard to the issue of -- the date, there may be a typo, but I would like to -- for the moment, I'd like to go --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could Mr. Guy_Smith straighten the microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I'd like to go to page number -- page number 12, if I could.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I understand your skepticism with regard to the issue of the information that you have thus far and your appreciation of the situation. If you look at page 12, I think you will note at the top it indicates that the areas Gorazde, that's where -- I think you were just referring to. And I have been informed that the language at the very top, that being Vazdusni Most is air bridge, Gorazde, and a then there are a series of dates that follow with regard to the assertion, at least, in this document of there being an air bridge at that time.
