But since you have not seen the document, I take it for what you said thus far, that you reject the notion out of hand that there would have been any kind of air support for the ABiH army in those enclaves. And by those enclave, I mean, Srebrenica, Zepa, and Gorazde.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Let's not embellish the witness's testimony. The witness said helicopters possibly, not aeroplanes. Therefore, there couldn't have been any air support.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I wonder if I might comment further, Your Honour. I would rule out of aircraft because of the absence of landing strips in these three enclaves.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Indeed. That's how I understood --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: And possible -- it would feasible to land a helicopter there. But even that, I'm very, very skeptical. I note also in the last page, I think page 12 that Mr. Guy-Smith brought my attention to, the first two alleged helicopter movements are on, representatively, the 15th and the 23th of April, 1994. Now the Court needs to be mindful of what the context was on those days. This was at the height of a Bosnian Serb military attack on the safe area of Gorazde. It was a period of intense military activity. Now, never were these helicopter movements or alleged movements reported to the UN by the Bosnian Serb forces because -- I mean, which I find surprising. They would have been quick off the mark normally to have reported anything like this. But also given the intensity of military action, the amount of firing and shelling that was going on, the close engagement by Serb artillery and armour, tanks, I find it very difficult to believe that a helicopter got in on either the 15th of April or the 23rd of April. The 23rd of April we were in Belgrade for talks with President Milosevic that Mr. Guy-Smith alluded to earlier. This was also a period when NATO aircraft were carrying out extremely close surveillance on the -- on the Gorazde area, and the fact that it was never reported to us, that they perceived or recorded helicopter or any other air movements is, I think, striking. So I have to say, I would seriously question the veracity of the information on this page, and in particular the two alleged flights on the 15th of April, 23rd of April.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: What is the basis of your scepticism that even helicopters could land there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, they could land there, Your Honour, but the fact that NATO was carrying out very, very close surveillance; the fact that military battle was going on, which, A, would have made it dangerous for the helicopters to land; and, B, that the Bosnian Serb forces, they never reported to us that the Bosnian army was violating the no-fly zone.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: You're not suggesting, are you, that helicopters don't land in theatres of operation where there's an ongoing conflict?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL CHARLES WILLIAMS
utterances.text: I'm -- I'm not suggesting that. But it's -- it's certainly more difficult to do that, when, by this stage, that particular week, the 15th to the 23rd of April, 1994, fighting was taking place at very close quarters in Gorazde, and I find it quite staggering that neither the Bosnian Serb forces nor the UN forces on the ground reported these helicopter movements to us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Williams, is that a period of a week, or a year? I think this period stretches from the 15th of April, 1994, to the 21st of April, 1995.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. The whole -- but the two cases I was referring to, in particular, Your Honour, were number 1 and 2.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's when the battle was at its most intense.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I'm with you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mm-hm.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Going to -- in view of the comments you've just made, and I appreciate the fact that you are at somewhat of a disadvantage because of the fact that this is not translated into English. I'm going to ask you whether or not the language that is contained on line number 2, and that is the very last entry, would change the testimony that you have just given. And I'm going to request that Mr. Lukic read for us in Serbian the language there so it can be translated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Which line 2 are you referring to, sir?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Where it says -- it says 2, and the date is the 23.4.94.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: What line 2, page?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: That would be page 12. I believe the page is up on the screen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Oh, you're looking at the exhibit. Not looking at the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I apologise. The page up on the screen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Because you talk about the language that he uses. That's why I'm looking at the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. With the assistance of Mr. Lukic, if you could please read for us in Serbian what it says there, the prekinat [phoen].

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, document marked 0185-4424, item number 2 says, 23rd of April, 1994. And in the last column, entitled "Remarks," it says mission aborted, helicopter hit. And the same is written under item 4. We have the same remark in the column and it says: Helicopter hit.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Considering what you just said about there being an active conflict at the time with regard to the first two entries and the fact that there was a war being waged at the moment as being a condition that would foreclose the use of helicopters, does that particular entry change the testimony that you have given us here today?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL CHARLES WILLIAMS
utterances.text: No, I don't believe it does, Mr. Guy-Smith.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I wonder if I might refer to an incident which is in the testimony I gave in the case against Mr. Milosevic in June 2003, which I think is related to this questioning from Mr. Guy-Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I don't have a problem with that in a moment. But I would like to follow up from where we were, first of all.

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL CHARLES WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: If the witness' answer is going to explain what he has just been asked, I think he might be given an opportunity to do so. Mr. Williams, can you please refer to the Milosevic testimony.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, what I was going to refer to was in that testimony I referred to an incident which also happens around this time in this week. I'm afraid I cannot recall the precise day, Your Honour, where two British soldiers serving with the United Nations were hit by incoming Serb fire. The UNPROFOR commander requested that he send into Gorazde an UN helicopter to medevac these two wounded soldiers out of Gorazde to hospital in Sarajevo. That took a long time negotiating with the Bosnian Serbs. It was eventually allowed. Tragically one of the soldiers died on the flight to Sarajevo from his injuries. The point I'm making is that even for the UN, it was impossible to send a helicopter into Gorazde at this point without the acceptance and permission of the Bosnian Serb military authorities. So I find it very, very difficult to believe that the Bosnian army would be able to infiltrate helicopters into a small town which, at this time, was a scene of intense battle.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: With regard to the -- the entry that is made there, assuming for purposes of discussion that the translation and entry are accurate, this, however, does change the complexion of your answer with regard to a helicopter being able to land in a conflict area, does it not? If the mission was aborted because the helicopter was shot, obviously there was an expectation that the helicopter didn't get in.

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL CHARLES WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Yes, I suppose so, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. Since we're on the subject of that which is in the air, I would like to talk to you for a moment about Tuzla. And, first of all, it's my understanding from your testimony that there was in fact an air strip at Tuzla that had been used, I think, sometime in the beginning of May of 1993. It was an area that was -- I believe it was designated as a safe area. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL CHARLES WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Correct, Mr. Guy-Smith. Tuzla is quite a large town in northern Bosnia. In May 1993, it was one of the six towns or -- that were designated safe areas by the Security Council under Resolution 836. There was a very substantial landing strip there and airport. In fact it had been, I think, a major military airport for the Yugoslav air force in pre-war days. Now, the UN had hoped to use this airport to supply Tuzla and the surrounding areas. And, indeed, I think, as was clear in my testimony, the UN did fly in one flight. I believe it was on the 1st of March, 1994, and I accompanied Mr. Akashi, the SRSG, on that flight. We had hoped to open an air bridge into Tuzla for supplying Tuzla itself and northern Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL CHARLES WILLIAMS
utterances.text: That proved impossible, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Were you aware of a visit by NATO officials and members of, amongst others, the United States air force, one Michael Hayden, the recently retired director from the CIA, in 1994, to the Tuzla air strip?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL CHARLES WILLIAMS
utterances.text: I'm not aware of that, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. Very good. That, we can take no further then. You use some very specific language in your testimony which is -- and I'm referring Court and counsel to page 22955, line 11: "What one saw was a fairly regular rotation of officers between the JA and Bosnian Serb forces and Croatian Serb forces." Because I'm sure there will be a dispute at some point later on if this is not clarified. With regard to the issue of JA here, are you referring to the JNA?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL CHARLES WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Yes, I am, Mr. Guy-Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I see. Okay. Thank you. With that taken care of, I have no further questions in that -- in that regard.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Could we please have up on the screen 1D00-1843. And if --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: First of all, per chance, are you familiar with this particular publication?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL CHARLES WILLIAMS
utterances.text: We put out a regular series of publications in English and also in -- in Serbo-Croat. I can't remember this one particularly. I mean, when I say we put them out on a sort of regular monthly basis, both in Croatia and Bosnia and also in Macedonia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Are you suggesting, Mr. Williams, that this is a UN document.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It could be, sir. I can't see a date on the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: If you don't know it, how do you even make that assumption? You can't recognise the document, but how do you assume it is an UN document?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honour, I didn't mean to assume it was. What I meant to state was --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Well, the question to you was, Do you know this document? And you say, We produced publications; I can't remember this one. Are you suggesting that it is one of those that you produced?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It may possibly be, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: That is it my question. Why do you go -- if you don't know it at all, do you or do you not know it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know it with any certainty, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Can I suggest that we try to answer the questions as succinctly as possible, because otherwise we get confused. We don't know what you really mean.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Understood, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: If we can go to page, I believe it is going to be page 13 of this document. And if we could -- thank you so much. If we can make it a little bit bigger, and if we can scroll -- scroll down.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: In -- do you see where the word "among" is?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL CHARLES WILLIAMS
utterances.text: The sentence beginning "among the most compelling of these ..."?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL CHARLES WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: It says: "Among the most compelling of these is the set of challenges surrounding the expanded 'peace menu,' including preventative diplomacy peacemaking, peacekeeping and peace-building."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The witness said he doesn't know this document. Didn't you want to at least get us to what this document is and where it comes from.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Sure. Okay, sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: This document is a document entitled "Peace Support Operations, Mass Media, and the Public in the Former Yugoslavia." It was written by Marjan Malesic and is a study, as I understand it, taken from -- by the national board of psychological defence in Sweden with regard to the role of the media in the conflict between Croatia and Serbia during a portion of the conflict.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I have a problem, Mr. Guy-Smith. That the witness says he doesn't know a document, and then you ask him a question. This happened with the last document which you didn't tender.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I didn't tender it, because as I said as I saw it there is no -- under the guidelines --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Can you please let me finish before you respond.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Sure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I'm saying this happened with the last document that you asked him extensive questions about it, and you read extensively from the document into the record, a document that he said he did not know anything about. You are doing the same thing here. And I think, obviously, if a witness says he doesn't know anything about a document, that's the end of the story about that document. You can't go on and ask him questions about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. I think that if the document contains information which is within the witness's purview, because they deal with concepts that are germane to the litigation at hand, that questions can be asked --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You can ask those questions without the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: But the document is --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Very well. I understand the Court's concern and the Court's objection. With that in mind, let's take the document off the screen. So we do not offend, because I don't wish to.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: With regard -- I'm going to posit a thought to you and ask you to respond, which is that, with regard to peace, that among the most compelling of these is a set of challenges surrounding the peace menu, including preventative diplomacy, peacemaking, peacekeeping, and peace-building. And what I'd like you to do, if could you, is define those terms, if you're in a position to, and give us what differences, if any, there might be between them. The first one being preventative diplomacy.

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL CHARLES WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Okay I will do my best in that regard. Preventative diplomacy a I would understand it in some sense, I mean, diplomats would argue -- some diplomats would argue that all diplomacy is preventative. That it's work by nation states or by the UN to prevent conflicts and disagreements before anything untoward happens. The second term you referred to is peacemaking.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Peacemaking, correct.

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL CHARLES WILLIAMS
utterances.text: That, I understand, to be almost self-explanatory, that one is trying to endeavour to make a peace agreement, whether it is between states in conflict or between factions in conflict. Thirdly, you refer me to peacekeeping, which can be -- again, keeping the peace between states or between warring factions. It can be on the basis of a formal agreement. It can be far more lose. And I'm afraid that that has been the pattern of many conflicts int he past 20 years or so. And then finally you refer to peace-building, which I understand as building after a conflict, perhaps after an agreement has been reached. In the Yugoslav context, for example, I would understand peace-building as something that has happened in the aftermath of the Dayton Agreement of 1995. I hope that helps.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I think it does. Can you help us at all with this, and perhaps you can; perhaps you can't. Do you find there to be any distinction between the function that the military performs in a peacekeeping, as opposed to peacemaking operation, or do you find them to be same?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL CHARLES WILLIAMS
utterances.text: I don't find them to be absolutely the same, but there is a grey area between the two. I mean, the dictionary definitions don't always stand in conflict situations on the ground.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. And with regard to the fact that you use the word "loose," and I here I don't want -- I don't want to misquote you. You said: "You refer me to peacekeeping, which can be keeping the peace between states or between warring factions. It can be on the basis of a formal agreement. It can be far more lose than" -- and I think what you said was, "which I'm afraid it has been over the past number of years. Now, with regard to the issue of that agreement being loose, are you talking about the agreement that exists between the warring factions, or are you referring to the agreement that exists between the peacekeeper?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL CHARLES WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Particularly between the warring factions and -- you know, even sometimes, dare I say it, mandates given to the UN by the Security Council are not as precise as one would always wish.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: With regard to the last point you raised here which is in terms of the mandates given to the UN by the Security Council, with regard to the conflict in Bosnia-Herzegovina, would you take the position that the mandate that was given to UNPROFOR was one of those mandates that lacked precision which caused difficulty over time?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL CHARLES WILLIAMS
utterances.text: There were certainly difficulties, Mr. Guy-Smith. And in a sense there was a succession of mandates because there was a succession of Security Council Resolutions. And all these were adopted by the Council over a period of several years whilst the conflict itself continued on the ground fairly unabated between 1992 and 1995. I mean, there were periods where there were lulls in the conflict, but more or less the conflict continued throughout that three-year period.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And with regard to what you just said, would it be fair to say that, first of all, this was a very unique situation; this is the first time that there had been this involvement of the international community in an ongoing conflict of the nature that existed between 1992 and 1995? I'm referring pretty much specifically to the actions of UNPROFOR.

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL CHARLES WILLIAMS
utterances.text: I'm trying to think that through and to give you as accurate an answer and response as -- as I can. As the Court will be aware, many of the conflicts in the world, since the end of the cold war in the late 1980s had been within states, often perhaps prompted by the breakup of states. So it is the case that often UN forces have been placed there to try and mitigate the consequences of these conflicts and to advance UN Resolutions.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Cyprus would be a good example of that, I would think. And I'm asking the question, and I see that you are probably going to take exception to that.

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL CHARLES WILLIAMS
utterances.text: I am, actually.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL CHARLES WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Because the Cyprus one is interesting, and as much as there was a conflict there, going back to 1974 and the Turkish invasion. UN forces are still there, 30 years on. The good new, as it were, is this is an agreement and there have been no incidents or violence of any sort really other than of an incidental nature in Cyprus. Now this was not the case in Bosnia, in the years in which, I believe, that the Court is dealing with here between 1992 and 1995, there was a fairly level of conflict. Now there are other cases where this is it the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And with regard to mandate, to the extent which was -- and I'm using a word which you may accept and you may well reject, and I understand that, but to the extent that there was internal confusion as to how best to proceed, did you experience that confusion manifesting itself in such a way as to leave a lack of clarity for the warring factions? You have to accept, first of all, the issue of the confusion before you can, I think, reach -- reach my question.

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL CHARLES WILLIAMS
utterances.text: I mean these were very difficult mandates. The situation on the ground was extraordinarily complex and was one, sadly, most of the time of continuing warfare. I'm afraid, Mr. Guy-Smith, I've lost the of end of your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Well, the point is, in your experience --

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL CHARLES WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Mm-hm.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: -- with the recognition of an internal confusion on the side of, what I will call, the international community as how best to proceed, did that confusion manifest itself so that the warring parties had a lack of clarity as to who precisely was standing for what?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL CHARLES WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Mm-hm, okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And perhaps if I put it in other terms. One of the words that has been used oftentimes in describing UNPROFOR is impartial. Another word is unbiased. Another word or concept is staying equal and not taking either side.

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL CHARLES WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Mm-hm. I think UNPROFOR strived to be impartial and unbiased, and I think it was. The Court needs to be aware, of course, that UNPROFOR was only deployed on the Bosnian government side of the battle lines, as it were. The Bosnian Serb authorities always would not tolerate any notion of UNPROFOR forces being deployed on their side of the battle lines. Some parts of the mandate were clearer than others; for example, the Resolution 836. Very clearly that identified safe areas and which were supposed to be not the scenes of conflict, and sadly all too often, they were.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: With regard to ultimatums that were made by UNPROFOR personnel that involved other organisations, such as NATO, did you, in your experience, negotiating through these troubled waters find that by virtue of the fact that there was a perceived connection between UNPROFOR and NATO, that there was a view that UNPROFOR was in fact biased by the Bosnian Serb leadership?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL CHARLES WILLIAMS
utterances.text: I mean, from time to time they would make that accusation. I think, you know, there are two specific ultimatum, or ultimata, or whatever the plural is, that you may be referring to. Following consistent attacks on Sarajevo by the Bosnian Serb army, NATO decided in February 1994 to give an ultimatum, that unless those attacks ceased, then NATO would conduct air-strikes against Bosnian Serb forces. There was a further ultimatum with regard to the enclave of Gorazde in April 1994. Now, those ultimatums came from NATO. NATO is a military alliance which is in a position, if it so wishes, to deliver those ultimatum. The UN and specifically UNPROFOR was not.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I note that you draw a distinction between the two, and I appreciate the distinction that you are drawing. However, it was common knowledge that -- was it not, that NATO's becoming involved was predicated upon UNPROFOR's request? And if it is of any help, we heard yesterday from Sir Rupert Smith with regard to this specific issue.

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL CHARLES WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Yes, it was. I mean, we talked earlier, for example, the question of helicopters and air movements and so on. UNPROFOR would not have been in a position to maintain a no-fly zone over Bosnia, for that you need fighter aircraft and you need radar and all of rest of it, and that was delivered by NATO, on request of the Security Council.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. I think that we may be dancing around each other a bit, and I don't mean to be at all. I'm driving at the issue of UNPROFOR being in the minds of the Bosnian Serb leadership, in your experience, I'm saying what they said to you, what you experienced in your contacts with them, that UNPROFOR and NATO, there was no distinction as between those two organisations in -- in their mind, as the way they were being treated.

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL CHARLES WILLIAMS
utterances.text: You know, sometimes they would make that accusation in the heat of argument, as it were; in particular, Mr. Karadzic, as I recall. But I think in reality they could see the distinction. UNPROFOR like any UN peacekeeping force drew its contingents from around the world, countries that were NATO countries, others which were not NATO countries, countries in Africa, countries in Asia, we had Indian, Indonesian forces, for example, Bangladesh forces. These were clearly not NATO forces. Also, the Bosnian Serbs were aware that the UN was also delivering, for example, humanitarian supplies on their side of the lines. So I -- I would not accept your assumption that they automatically saw NATO and UNPROFOR as the same thing or ...

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Well, I'm sorry, it's not my assumption. My question was what was your experience? And that's really what I was getting at. And I think you have answered that particular question, that it's something that happened -- it happened on some occasions, but it was, in your view, not something that was necessarily a prevalent theme with regard to the Bosnian Serb leadership in their discussions with you.

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL CHARLES WILLIAMS
utterances.text: That's correct, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: If we might break at this time, so that I have the opportunity to speak specifically with our client. He has a great interest in this particular examination, and I want to make sure that those matters have been attended to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: We'll take a break and come back at half past 12.00. Court adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Guy-Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you. I would like to thank the Chamber for the additional five minutes. It was most helpful.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. You're welcome.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: You were asked a question here today. It's a question that you were asked in your previous testimony as well, with regard to your concerns about the humanitarian crisis, and specifically you were asked about tangible objective signs. And you indicated, that your estimation is, as certainly as early as February that concern was not only a concern that you had, but also a concern, as I understood your testimony, that other members of the international community had. Correct?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL CHARLES WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Correct, sir. Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Also, it was a concern that Mr. Milosevic had expressed as well.

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL CHARLES WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And, as a matter of fact, I believe that Milosevic had stated that -- that he concurred that the situation in Bosnia and Herzegovina would deteriorate. True?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL CHARLES WILLIAMS
utterances.text: I recall him saying that, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And the question really was where -- and this is still talking about in February. This was where the responsibility for the deterioration would lay. And by that, I mean, Milosevic blamed it on the international community's focus on, as I understand it, details and not the situation as a whole. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL CHARLES WILLIAMS
utterances.text: That would be the gist of his argument, I think, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Thomas.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honour. I wonder if we could just have some clarification. February of what year?

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Now, with regard to the matter at hand, and by that I mean the tangible concern that existed, were you involved in your capacity with any plans to militarily take over the area from -- by the international community so as to foreclose these concerns?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL CHARLES WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Not at all, Mr. Guy-Smith. I'm not quite sure, militarily take over what area now?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Srebrenica. There was a concern that you had, and the question that was asked was where there's tangible objective signs, that if the enclave of Srebrenica were to fall --

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL CHARLES WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Mm-hm.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: -- there would be a humanitarian crisis on a grand scale?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL CHARLES WILLIAMS
utterances.text: I understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL CHARLES WILLIAMS
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... Correct. I understand your question, now, sorry, I didn't earlier.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL CHARLES WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Throughout the period I served in former Yugoslavia, and particularly in Bosnia and Herzegovina, there were a series of military operations against the UN Safe Areas, four in particular. Number one being Sarajevo in February 1994; Gorazde in April 1994; Bihac in late 1994; and then, of course, finally, Srebrenica. In all cases we had concerns, well grounded concerns, about the civilian inhabitants of the safe areas and what would become of them in the light of Serb attacks, let alone a Serb seizure of one of these safe areas. Now, as the Court knows this only happened in one case, Srebrenica, and to a lesser extent, Zepa in summer of 1995. But I have to say that in the conduct of the military operations, on many occasions the Bosnian Serbs gave grave concern that their military actions broke accepted practices of international humanitarian law. And this was seen in Sarajevo and in Gorazde in 1994, and for this reason, we were always extraordinarily apprehensive when there were Serb attacks on safe areas.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: That's understood. As I understand the complexion of the situation, certainly in February, you had Milosevic attempting to influence the Bosnian Serbs for peace. You had the international community attempting to influence the Bosnian Serbs for peace. And much of these entreaties were falling on deaf ears?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL CHARLES WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Sadly, the case, Mr. Guy-Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I would concur with you, it being sadly the case. In the months that ensued the conflict between the Bosnian Serbs and the BiH army increased; correct?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL CHARLES WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And it would be fair to say that both parties calcified, from the standpoint of opting for war as opposed to obtaining a peaceful solution?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL CHARLES WILLIAMS
utterances.text: I wouldn't agree with you entirely, and I think to illustrate why we need to revisit the concept of the safe areas. As I indicated earlier this mourning in my testimony, these were established by Security Council Resolution 836. Much of the military activity consisted of attacks by the BSA on the Serb areas. Now, this is it not to say, this is not say that there were not occasions firing from within the safe areas on Bosnian Serb positions. But I would say that this -- such outgoing fire, as it were, was much lighter than the attacks pursued by Bosnian Serb forces. I feel also I should draw the Court' attention to the disproportionality and the armament of the relevant sides. That, on the Bosnian Serb side, artillery, armour, helicopters, even ground air missile defence systems were deployed. None of this armament was available to the ABiH side, or, if it was, only in very small an incidental quantities. So there is there was a disproportion between the two fighting forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Yes, I understand that. But once again, what I was driving at is that both sides had made the determination and that the option was -- was war, not peace. And we heard yesterday from Sir Rupert Smith concerning this matter, that there came a point -- I mean, he had a thesis about that. But there certainly came a point where there were a continuing of ABiH offensives throughout the spring and summer months of 1995.

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL CHARLES WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. And, finally, I wanted to read you a question and an answer of your previous testimony to be found at 22967, starting at line 10. "Question: In your view, as of February 1995, did Milosevic equally appreciate the gravity of the situation in Bosnia?" And your answer: "I think he did. We were stumbling all the time from one crisis to another, from Sarajevo in February 1994, to the Gorazde crisis in April 1994, to Bihac in October/November. And it was obvious given the continued deterioration, and on the ground in Bosnia and around the eastern enclaves that one could premise a further crisis and deterioration in 1995." I trust that you continue to stand by that remark.

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL CHARLES WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: That's what we were talking about just before.

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL CHARLES WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Yes, I definitely do, Mr. Guy-Smith, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And if I'm not mistaken, this remark takes also into account that an appreciation of the gravity of the situation by the leadership of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia embodied in Slobodan Milosevic?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL CHARLES WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Yes, I think it does.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: All right. Thank you much, sir, for your time and your candor.

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL CHARLES WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Thomas.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have no questions in re-examination. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Judge?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PICARD
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have a question to ask. You had several meetings with Milosevic. You were present at those meetings with Mr. Milosevic in Belgrade. According to what you observed, did Milosevic seem informed of what was going on in -- in Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL CHARLES WILLIAMS
utterances.text: I think, on the whole, Your Honour, he was very well informed of what was going on. Some of the detail maybe he didn't know. I recall in particular the meeting, or meetings, over 18 hours on April 22nd and 23rd, 1994, in Belgrade during the Gorazde crisis, where he was looking for a solution and showing some irritation, visible irritation, with the Bosnian Serbs at their behaviour in continuing to attack the Gorazde enclave.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PICARD
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have a second question, and if you can't answer, just say so. You said that -- that the FRY helped the Serbs of Bosnia, the Serbian army in Bosnia. And you said that, nevertheless, if there was no control on this army, there was a great influence from Milosevic on what was going on with the Serbs in Bosnia. So my question is the following. As from the moment when Milosevic -- or at least the FRY was helping the army, the Serbian army in Bosnia, and from the moment Milosevic knew what was going on in Bosnia, according to you, why didn't he exert more pressure, in particular, practical pressure, material pressure, on the Serbian leaders in Bosnia to try precisely to stop this? Since you said yourself that he wasn't in agreement with what was going on.

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL CHARLES WILLIAMS
utterances.text: A difficult question, Your Honour. Sometimes, dare I say it, statesman are not always as honest as they should be in their responses. Certainly Mr. Milosevic said the right things about wishing to attain peace in Bosnia, and I think he did strive on some occasions to -- to realize that. Against that, it is very difficult not to conclude that the Bosnian Serb army was -- was receiving substantial logistical assistance from the FRY. In fact, during the course of 1994/1995 one witnessed that their military capabilities actually increased. For example, the deployment of ground to air missile systems, which are very, very advanced in the Sarajevo area and which would necessitated radar and missile systems being reconciled and so on. And clearly the Bosnian Serb forces were receiving assistance in this regard, and one has to assume that it was coming from the FRY. But I cannot reconcile the contradiction that you duly noted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PICARD
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... questions arising from the questions by the Judge?

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: No, sir. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Guy-Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: During 1994/1995, were you aware of illegal, and by that I mean other nations or entities, supplying weapons to either side, either the Bosnian Serb army or the BiH?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL CHARLES WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Yes -- yes, I was, Mr. Guy-Smith. First of all, with regard to the BiH, the Bosnian army, there was quite specific allegations and reports that their forces in Bihac, in north western Bosnia, were receiving supplies from Croatia, either by land, or, in some cases, even by air. This was an enclave which directly abutted Croatian territory, so it was easily supplied in that sense, and there were reports of movements by land and by air that were documented by UN forces. With regard to the Bosnian Serb forces, one saw them deploy very sophisticated weapon systems, artillery, armour, helicopters, ground-to-air missiles which had to be supplied from somewhere, and I never saw an allegation that they were receiving weaponry from any source other than from the FRY itself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The -- okay. Carry on.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: At line 69, you indicated and one?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: We don't have a line 69.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Sorry, page 69, line 1, you indicated the -- one has to assume that Serbian forces were receiving assistance in that regard, and it was coming from the FRY. You used the word "assume." And it's that where I wish to focus. And I take it that your conclusion is based upon an assumption that that is where the materiel was coming from because of sophistication.

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL CHARLES WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Sophistication, the fact that armies are very resource-intensive.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Understood.

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL CHARLES WILLIAMS
utterances.text: They need fuel; they need arms; they need constant replenishment. And this has to come from somewhere.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Understood. And with regard to the sophisticated weaponry, you've told us that weapons were being received from Croatia. And when you say from Croatia, do you mean Croatia proper, the government? Or do you mean through the territory of Croatia?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL CHARLES WILLIAMS
utterances.text: This is a bit more -- definitely from the territory of Croatia, of that there was no doubt. And of course, in 1994, the relationship between Croats and Muslims within Bosnia improved, and also the relationship between Croatia and Bosnia itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL CHARLES WILLIAMS
utterances.text: So that provided, as it were, political context, which perhaps enabled arms supplies to one area in particular, the Bihac area of north-western Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I understand that. But once again you're making an assumption, and that is that the supplies, the weapons -- and when you said supplies, I take it you also meant weapons. Because I certainly don't wish to put any words in your mouth, because it would be confusing to the Chamber, in any way whatsoever. You're making an assumption that supplies that came from Croatia by virtue of the relationship between the Croatians and the Muslims were from the Croatian government, perhaps, or from the Croatian military. That's an assumption that you're making.

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL CHARLES WILLIAMS
utterances.text: It's an assumption. But -- and from the government or from agencies with -- within the government, and there were some flights recorded from Croatia into to Bihac. And it's difficult not to conclude that some of these may have been known to departments of the Croatian government.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. So that would be -- that would shift the position of where the genesis of the weaponry comes from, to the knowledge that the Croatian government may well have had with regard to the weaponry passing through their territory; correct?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL CHARLES WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Correct, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Now, with regard to this particular issue, the issue of the supply of weapons, there were allegations made that the United States was supplying weapons; correct?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL CHARLES WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And, as a matter of fact, there were allegations made --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Thomas.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honours, first of all, my learned friend hasn't been particular about who the United States was supposed to -- or who the allegations say the US were supplying weapons to.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I'm not suggesting that they were -- that they were being supplied to one side or the other, just that they were being supplied. The issue here that I'm getting at is that there were a series of allegations made with regard to the supplying of weapons to both the ABiH and to the Bosnian Serb army from sources other than Croatia or FRY.

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL CHARLES WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Yes, there were allegations, yeah.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Thomas.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: Sorry. Before this continues any further, Your Honours, I'm very conscious that this is now strayed quite far from the original question asked by Her Honour, which was limiting, which was the question of whether -- and I'll find it so that I can quote it probably, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I believe if you go to page 68.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: Which about the supply of the VRS, specifically the supply of the VRS and that it came from the FRY. There was some initial questions now about the supply of the ABiH, but now we just seem be getting further and further down that path, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Guy-Smith asked whether there were any other supplies of arms and ammunition to either side, and I understood the word "other" to mean other than supplies from the FRY. Now, if there are any allegations that the US was also supplying arms that's a source other than the FRY, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: I have no difficulty with that questioning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: What you're difficulty? Because I haven't heard any objectionable ground in -- what's your ground of objection?

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: The sourcing of the ABiH army.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The source?

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: The sourcing or the supply of the ABiH army. This is a new element that has now emerged in the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Because the Judge didn't refer to -- supply to ABiH.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Guy-Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Well, I asked the question by virtue of the response that was given by the witness, that he said the supplies were coming through Croatia. I do not need to dwell on that part of it. I think have I gotten as far as I need to go with that particular issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: In response to Her Honour's question, I'm now dealing finally with the specific language on page 68, line 24, which is, you say, one has to assume, and my question to you is what you're doing here is you are speculating with regard to where the particular supplies came from?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You asked that question, and he told you his grounds for his assumption. Now you're going back --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Now I'm asking him specifically as to whether it was speculative. And that is my last question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honour, should I proceed?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You may proceed, sir.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There was no doubt that the weaponry deployed in 1994/1995 by the VRS, by the Bosnian Serb army, included very sophisticated weapons platforms not available to other forces, like the ABiH. I have never seen a report or even an allegation that the VRS was supplied by some force other than Yugoslavia or other than Serbia, and no indication whatsoever of -- of that. One has to pose the question, therefore, that given an increase in armaments to the Bosnian Serb forces during this period, from whence did this come? Now much earlier in my testimony this morning, I talked about a sort of political break between the Bosnian republic and -- leadership and the Yugoslav leadership of Mr. Milosevic. By contrast there were very close ties, I think, between the Yugoslav army of the FRY and the VRS of the Bosnian Serb republic. There had never been the sort of rupture that there had been on the political level between Belgrade and Pale. The two armies came out of the original army; namely, the Yugoslav national army before the breakup of Yugoslavia. So there was an intimacy from the very fact that the officer course, the logistics bases, these had always been one at a certain time. And it is my belief that that past was never completely broken with. And it is from that that I make the deduction that the supplies of the VRS must have come from the FRY.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I had indicated that that would be my last question. However, the answer --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Go ahead, Mr. Guy-Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: In your answer, you said, I have never seen a report or even an allegation. And so I take it that by virtue of that, we're proving a negative here, in the manner that you have put it.

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL CHARLES WILLIAMS
utterances.text: They have to come from somewhere. One can look at the map, one can study the history, one can know the personal ties between the two military leaderships, one can know that they adopted similar military and technical strategies and so on, and I think, at the end of the day, one can make a deduction from this, which is what I have tried to do.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL CHARLES WILLIAMS
utterances.text: In all honesty.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And perhaps not finally, but hopefully so, with regard to the Republika Srpska, there was an Assembly and a president; correct?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL CHARLES WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Correct, Mr. Guy-Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: There were a full set of laws that existed, including laws that created an army; correct?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL CHARLES WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And General Mladic had a Supreme Commander, that being the president of the Republika Srpska, Mr. Radovan Karadzic; correct?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I think you must get to the point, Mr. Guy-Smith. There has been no questions about that by the Judge. And if you're making a foundation, get to the point quickly.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Can I get an answer to my last question, please.

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL CHARLES WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Correct, Mr. Guy-Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: In fact, what you had was the formation of an independent military structure that was operated by and commanded by General Mladic. True?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL CHARLES WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Correct. But this doesn't come from nowhere, and it wasn't born on day one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Can you give us the relevance, please, the relevance to the questions asked by the Judge?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: It's relevant to an answer that he gave.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Which answer?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: The answer that is contained at page 74, lines 2 through 23. And that is my last question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Lines 2, 3.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I mean, the argument, in terms of the issue of relevance, whether or not you have similar military structures or not, whether or not you have individuals who have grown up together or gone to school together does not necessarily take one to the point of making a determination of there being certain kinds of relationships between them --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: You asked me what the relevance was, so I'm responding to your question. That was the relevance of my question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I still don't see the relevance.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. Well, the relevance of my question deals the fact that if there is an independent military structure, as I'm sure the Chamber is aware having sat in previous trials, and as we will certainly learn here, there's certain rules and regulations that must be followed with regard to that military structure. And so to the extent that you have fellow -- you have friends who have known each other for a long time, it doesn't necessarily impact and make a logical deduction that something would be necessarily true.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: It doesn't make a logical deduction, but the witness has given you a number of facts on which he bases his inferences. And I think the inference he is making is that where there is close relationship between the people, the likelihood is that they will help one another.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I understand that -- [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... And that has nothing to do with the structure of the military in the RS.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: But I think ultimately at a point in time in terms of these proceedings it will. Because at some point in time the Chamber is going to have to address this question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: It is very clear that some of the questions that have come from the Chamber deal with this very issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Indeed.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And there is clearly a concern about this particular issue. And to the extent that at some point we're going to be dealing with inferences and questions of structure as well friendships are going to be central to that analysis is the reason why this question was asked at that time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: What I'm saying that is structure has nothing to do with friendships. For purposes of relevance here.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. We disagree on that, but that will come into light at a later point in time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The witness refers to structure separately and referred to friendship separately. He did say that the VRS came from the JNA -- or didn't use the word JNA, however, but he said it came from the same army, which may have referred to this -- the beginnings of the VRS. Then he told about close relationships and that the relationships were never -- he doesn't think that the relationships were ever broken.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I appreciate that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I still think we have a difference of opinion in terms of where this ultimately goes, but I understand precisely what the Court's thinking is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: On that note, Mr. Williams, thank you so much for taking time off from you schedule for coming to testimony. This brings us to the end of your testimony. You are now excused. You may stand down. Please travel well back home.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Thomas.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. First of all, I can indicate that the redaction that was required to Mr. Williams's statement has been done, and I'm advised that the appropriate version has now been uploaded into e-court. And therefore I would seek that Exhibit P2371 -- or that the MFI status of P2371 be removed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: It is so removed. May it please be removed, Madam Registrar. Yes, Mr. Thomas.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The status will be changed to exhibit, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Secondly the transcript, P23727 should, at this stage, remain an MFI exhibit. I've discussed it with my learned friend. I'm confident that we'll be able to resolve this. But it will need us to just consider one or two extracts or one or two portions of that transcript. As I said, Your Honour, I'm optimistic that we can advise in due course that that has all been resolved, and it can be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: It hadn't been admitted, had it?

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: It had, sir. 2372.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: So you want it to remain MFI?

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: I do. Yes, sir. And that concludes finally, sir, the evidence for this week. The next witness is scheduled for Monday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Then the Chamber stands adjourned to Monday, the 25th of May, at quarter past 2.00, in Courtroom I. Court adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Monday, the 25th day of May, 2009, at 2.15 p.m.
